extracted.intended_audience: mathematics educators, education researchers, curriculum developers, and graduate students
extracted.subtask_description: Framework and literature-driven criteria for what it means to think mathematically and for designing/assessing instruction that fosters mathematical problem solving, metacognition, and sense-making. The chapter reviews definitions, cognitive components, pedagogical implications, and assessment directions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematics as sense-making / mathematical point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning to think mathematically means (a) developing a mathematical point of view — valuing the processes of mathematization and abstraction and having the predilection to apply them, and (b) developing competence with the tools of the trade, and using those tools in the service of the goal of understanding structure — mathematical sense-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize valuing mathematization and abstraction, using abstraction/symbolic representation to understand structure rather than merely learning procedures; teaching should foster an orientation to see problems as opportunities for sense-making, not only drill on techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem types: routine versus nonroutine
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish problems that are routine exercises (tasks required to be done; practiced procedures) from problems that are perplexing or difficult (real problem solving).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate curriculum and instruction by the balance and role of routine practice vs. engagement with nonroutine, challenging problems. The chapter documents that many 'problem solving' efforts were actually routine-practice repackaging (anti-pattern). Use examples (Milne exercises) to identify routine structure: introduce technique, illustrate, give practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roles of problems in instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems can serve multiple roles: (1) as a justification for teaching mathematics, (2) to provide specific motivation for subject topics, (3) as recreation (motivation), (4) as a means of developing new skills, and (5) as practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing tasks, be explicit which role is intended. Avoid treating all problems merely as practice for procedural mastery when the instructional goal is cultivating heuristic thinking or sense-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristics / problem-solving strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Problem solving strategies (heuristics) such as drawing diagrams, looking for patterns (n = 1,2,3...), and other 'modern heuristics' are central techniques to teach; Pólya's notion of plausible reasoning and guessing plays a central role in discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach heuristics embedded in practice; emphasize assimilation so heuristics become 'ready for instant use.' Provide opportunities for guessing, modification, and plausible reasoning rather than only presenting formal rules. Beware of teaching heuristics only as isolated rules without practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resources / core knowledge and cognitive architecture
rubrics_metrics.description: Thinking mathematically relies on cognitive resources: core knowledge, constructive nature of cognition, memory structures, and access to these resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction and assessment should consider how students store, retrieve, and construct knowledge; research/assessment should examine memory, representation, and how students access relevant knowledge. Recognize limits (e.g., working memory) when designing tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitoring and control (metacognition / self-regulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Metacognition involves monitoring and control — self-regulation during problem solving (planning, monitoring, evaluating one’s solution processes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foster and assess students' ability to monitor their work, detect impasses, strategize adjustments, and reflect. Consider metacognitive prompts, scaffolds, and microgenetic analyses; recognize metacognition has multiple meanings and operationalize it clearly for instruction/assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beliefs and affect
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals' beliefs, dispositions, and affective relationships to mathematics (e.g., confidence, anxiety, sense of control) fundamentally influence mathematical behavior and performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend to students' epistemological beliefs and affective states in instruction and assessment. Interventions should address math anxiety, perceived control, and beliefs about the nature of math (fixed vs. sense-making).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enculturation and social practices (cognitive apprenticeship)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics learning is inherently social and constructive; developing a mathematical point of view arises through enculturation into communities of practice and legitimate peripheral participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design instruction that creates microcosms of mathematical practice (collaborative problem solving, apprenticeship models). Evaluate programs by how well they socialize students into mathematical norms and practices rather than merely transmit procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical epistemology ↔ pedagogy linkage
rubrics_metrics.description: Pedagogy should mirror mathematical epistemology: if mathematics is a practice involving guessing, discovery, and plausible reasoning, classrooms must provide opportunities for such activity so students' experience aligns with how mathematics is done.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide tasks that require conjecturing, proof sketches, and iterative refinement. Avoid pure formalistic presentation disconnected from discovery processes; assess whether learning experiences reflect authentic mathematical epistemology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructional structure and its implicit assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: A common instructional structure for routine problem sets: (a) A task introduces a technique; (b) technique is illustrated; (c) more tasks provide practice. The basic assumption is that mastery of techniques equates to mathematical understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this rubric to critique curricula: if instruction follows the introduce-illustrate-practice template exclusively, it may produce procedural mastery without deeper understanding (anti-pattern). Consider alternative structures that promote sense-making and transfer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goals for mathematics instruction (curricular emphases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructional goals should include seeking solutions (not just memorizing procedures), exploring patterns (not just memorizing formulas), and formulating conjectures (not just doing exercises).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Align curricula, pedagogy, and assessment toward these emphases (as recommended by EverybodyCounts and NCTM). Use tasks and assessments that require exploration, conjecture, and explanation rather than only procedural fluency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment aligned with mathematical thinking goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Specification of new assessment techniques is required to determine whether students are achieving goals consonant with learning to think mathematically (problem solving, metacognition, sense-making).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop assessment methods that probe heuristics use, metacognitive control, beliefs, and the ability to engage in mathematical practices; preliminary steps and microgenetic analyses are suggested. Avoid relying solely on instrument measures of routine procedural tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical power / quantitative literacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematically powerful students are quantitatively literate: able to interpret quantitative data, make balanced judgments, use mathematics in practical ways, and approach novel problems with flexible repertoires and analytical thinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction and assessment should aim for transfer to real-world contexts and flexibility, measuring students' ability to apply mathematical thinking to varied, authentic tasks.
